questions.question: A two-variable integer model is to be solved graphically. Which procedure does graphical integer programming follow?
options: Plot the continuous constraints, find the best corner, then round it to the nearest lattice point
Plot the continuous constraints, then compare the objective at the feasible lattice points
Plot the continuous constraints, then compare the objective at all corners of the region
Plot only the integer points, ignoring the constraints, and take the best objective value

questions.question: For a two-variable integer model, the best corner of the continuous feasible region is $(2.5,4)$. What is the status of $(2.5,4)$ for the integer model?
options: It is optimal, since it is the best corner of the region
It is permitted, as one of its coordinates is an integer
It becomes the integer optimum after rounding $x_1$ up to $3$
It is not a permitted decision, since $x_1$ is fractional

questions.question: In a two-variable linear program with an optimum, an optimal corner of the feasible region exists. Which statement about the best lattice point of a two-variable integer model is correct?
options: The best lattice point is always a corner of the region.
The best lattice point need not be a corner of the region.
The best lattice point always lies on at least one constraint line.
The best lattice point is always the one nearest to the best corner.

questions.question: A two-variable integer model has a bounded continuous feasible region containing 12 lattice points. Why does comparing the objective at all 12 points prove optimality?
options: The best of them is a corner, and corners are always optimal
They are all the permitted decisions, so the best is optimal
The objective line through any one of them shows the optimum
Any 12 checked lattice points suffice, even in a large region

questions.question: An integer model requires $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer, and $(3,2.5)$ satisfies all its linear constraints. Is $(3,2.5)$ feasible for the model?
options: No, because $x_2=2.5$ is not an integer
Yes, because it satisfies the linear constraints
No, because feasible points must lie on a constraint line
Yes, after $x_2$ is rounded down to 2

questions.question: An integer model has constraints $x_1+2x_2\le7$, $3x_1+x_2\le9$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer. Which point is feasible?
The integer model $\max 2x_1+x_2$ subject to $2x_1+3x_2\le12$, $x_1\le4$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer is solved graphically. Which point is optimal?

For the integer model $\max 3x_1+2x_2$ subject to $2x_1+2x_2\le9.5$, $x_1\le3.5$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer, the best corner of the continuous region is $(3.5,1.25)$. Rounding each coordinate to the nearest integer gives $(4,1)$. Which statement about $(4,1)$ is correct?
options: It breaks both $2x_1+2x_2\le9.5$ and $x_1\le3.5$
It breaks $x_1\le3.5$ but satisfies $2x_1+2x_2\le9.5$
It fails integrality, since $x_1$ came from rounding
It is feasible, and its value 14 beats $(3,1)$

questions.question: The integer model $\max x_1+x_2$ subject to $2x_1+3x_2\le12$, $x_1\le4$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer is solved graphically. What is its optimal value?
The integer model $\min 2x_1+3x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\ge3.5$, $x_1\le3$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer is solved graphically. Which lattice point has the lowest cost?

A two-variable maximization model is solved twice: once over its continuous feasible region with optimal value $v_C$, and once with integer restrictions added, giving optimal value $v_I$. How do $v_I$ and $v_C$ compare?
options: $v_I\ge v_C$, as integer points are easier to compare
$v_I\le v_C$, as the lattice points lie in the region
$v_I=v_C$, as both use the same constraints
Either can be larger; the two problems are unrelated

questions.question: For a two-variable integer maximization model, the graphical method on the continuous region gives a unique optimal corner. In which case does that corner immediately solve the integer model?
options: When both coordinates of the corner are integers
When all constraint coefficients are integers
When the continuous region is bounded
When the objective coefficients are integers

questions.question: An integer model $\max x_1+x_2$ has the single constraint $x_1-x_2\le1.5$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer. A student checks 30 lattice points and reports the best one as optimal. Why is that not a proof?
options: Thirty points prove optimality only if one of them is a corner
Thirty points suffice if they include every lattice point next to the constraint line
The region is unbounded, so there are infinitely many lattice points
Lattice points cannot be compared when a constraint has a fraction

questions.question: The integer model $\max 5x_1+4x_2$ subject to $6x_1+4x_2\le24$, $x_1+2x_2\le6$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer has continuous optimum $(3,1.5)$ with value 21. Which point is optimal for the integer model?
options: $(3,1)$ with value 19
$(3,2)$ with value 23
$(4,0)$ with value 20
$(3,1.5)$ with value 21

questions.question: The integer model $\max x_1+x_2$ subject to $2x_1+3x_2\le12$, $x_1\le4$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer is solved by comparing lattice points. Which set lists all optimal points?

For the integer model $\max 3x_1+2x_2$ subject to $2x_1+2x_2\le9.5$, $x_1\le3.5$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer, the best lattice point is $(3,1)$ with value 11. The right-hand side $9.5$ is lowered to $8$. What is the new optimal value of the integer model?

For the integer model $\max 3x_1+2x_2$ subject to $2x_1+2x_2\le9.5$, $x_1\le3.5$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer, the best lattice point $(3,1)$ satisfies both constraints strictly, as $8<9.5$ and $3<3.5$. What does this show?
options: $(3,1)$ cannot be optimal, as no constraint is binding.
The constraint $x_1\le3.5$ can be dropped without effect.
Integer optima are always strictly inside the region.
A best lattice point can have slack in every constraint.

questions.question: In a bounded two-variable integer maximization model, a feasible lattice point $\boldsymbol{p}$ has a higher objective value than every feasible lattice point next to it (one step in either coordinate). Must $\boldsymbol{p}$ be optimal?
options: Yes; no neighbour of $\boldsymbol{p}$ improves the value.
Yes, if $\boldsymbol{p}$ also lies on a constraint line.
No; a better lattice point can lie several steps away.
Only when the objective coefficients are all equal.

questions.question: For the integer model $\max 3x_1+2x_2$ subject to $2x_1+2x_2\le9.5$, $x_1\le3.5$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer, the objective line $3x_1+2x_2=v$ is moved from $v=13$, through the best corner $(3.5,1.25)$, towards smaller $v$. At which level does it first meet a feasible lattice point?

For $\max x_1+4x_2$ subject to $x_1+5x_2\le12$, $4x_1-3x_2\le14$, $x_1,x_2\ge0$ integer, the continuous optimum is about $(4.61,1.48)$. A student checks only the four lattice points around it. What is the actual optimal point?
options: $(4,1)$ with value 8
$(5,1)$ with value 9
$(2,2)$ with value 10
$(4,2)$ with value 12
